title: An atom and its electron cloud
alt: A live 3D view of the electron of a hydrogen atom in an s state: a cloud of dots where it is likely to be found, the surface where its wavefunction has one fixed size and, from n = 2 on, the spherical radial node shells where it is never found. Beside it, the curve of the probability of finding the electron at each distance from the nucleus, with the most probable distance marked.
sentences: An atom is a nucleus with electrons around it, but an electron is not a tiny ball on an orbit.
Quantum mechanics gives a cloud of probability instead: the 3D view shows that cloud around the nucleus, and the curve beside it shows how likely the electron is to be found at each distance.
Everything later in DFT is about these clouds, and about how they overlap and rearrange when atoms meet.

title: A wavefunction and an orbital
alt: A live 3D view of one hydrogen orbital as the surface where its wavefunction has one fixed size, orange where it is positive and blue where it is negative: a round s orbital, a p orbital with two lobes, or a d orbital (3d z2) with two lobes and a ring. Beside it, a slice through the same kind of orbital's cloud.
sentences: The wavefunction is the quantity that holds everything about one electron, and an orbital is the shape of one allowed wavefunction.
The s cloud is a ball, the p clouds have two lobes, and the d clouds are more complex still.
These shapes decide which neighbouring atoms an electron can bond with, which is why they matter for materials.

title: The exponential wall
alt: Curve of how fast the number of values needed to describe many electrons together grows as electrons are added, rising far faster than a straight line.
sentences: Describing N electrons exactly, all together, needs a number of values that grows exponentially with N.
The curve counts the values needed on a coarse grid as electrons are added, and it soon passes anything a computer could store.
That wall is why DFT replaces the many-electron problem with something much smaller.

title: Density as a map
alt: Map of electron density along a box for a chosen number of electrons, higher where the electrons are more likely to be.
sentences: Instead of following every electron, DFT follows one map: how much electron charge sits at each point in space.
The picture is the density of electrons in a one-dimensional box, and its shape follows the levels that the electrons fill.
A theorem of Hohenberg and Kohn says that, in principle, this one map is enough to fix the ground-state energy.

try.label: Number of electrons in the box

title: The Kohn-Sham idea
alt: A one-dimensional toy atom showing the electron density and, optionally, the effective potential that the density produces, after a self-consistent run.
sentences: Kohn and Sham replaced the hard problem by electrons that do not see each other directly but move in one shared effective potential.
That potential depends on the density, and the density comes from the electrons moving in it, so the two must agree with each other.
The picture is a one-dimensional toy model and not a real calculation.

title: The self-consistency loop
alt: Curve of how much the electron density changes from one step of a toy self-consistency loop to the next, falling as the loop settles.
sentences: Guess a density, build the potential from it, solve for the electrons, and compare the new density with the guess.
Repeat until the density stops changing; the curve shows how the change shrinks from step to step in a toy model.
In this toy model a larger mixing fraction settles in fewer steps; real calculations can behave differently, so VASP's mixing settings are worth knowing.

title: The crystal and its unit cell
alt: A cube-based unit cell with its atoms drawn inside the cell edges.
sentences: A crystal is one small block of atoms, the unit cell, repeated in every direction.
The box in the picture is the cell; its lengths and angles and the positions of the atoms inside it are all that VASP needs to know about the structure.
Change the cell type to see how one idea gives different arrangements of atoms.

title: Periodic images
alt: Rock-salt unit cell shown once or repeated in all directions, so that the same block of atoms appears in every neighbouring cell.
sentences: VASP treats your cell as repeating forever, so an atom that leaves one side comes back in on the opposite side.
Repeating the cell in the picture shows this: every copy holds the same atoms in the same places.
That is why a small cell can stand in for a whole crystal, and why a molecule needs empty space around it so that its copies do not interact.

title: Plane waves and the ENCUT sphere
alt: Curve of plane-wave energy against wavevector with a horizontal cutoff line, keeping the waves below the line and dropping the ones above it.
sentences: VASP writes each electron's wavefunction as a sum of plane waves, which are simple waves that repeat across the cell.
ENCUT sets the largest plane-wave energy that is kept; on the picture the cutoff line separates the waves that are kept from the ones that are dropped.
A higher cutoff keeps more waves and costs more time, and a cutoff that is too low gives unreliable energies, which is why you test it.

title: Reciprocal space and the Brillouin zone
alt: The three real-space lattice vectors of a face-centred cubic cell and the three reciprocal vectors that go with them, drawn in one picture.
sentences: Every crystal has a partner space called reciprocal space, where the repeating pattern is described by waves instead of positions.
Its repeat unit is the Brillouin zone, and each point in the zone is a k-point: one wave pattern that electrons in the crystal can have.
The picture shows the real-space cell vectors with the reciprocal vectors that match them; only directions and relative lengths are meaningful.

title: k-points: sampling the zone
alt: A live 3D view of a regular grid of k-points filling the cubic Brillouin zone of a simple cubic crystal, with the points that symmetry makes different marked larger; beside it, the same kind of grid laid over a square zone. The slider sets the number of points along each direction.
sentences: VASP cannot visit every k-point, so it samples the zone on a regular grid, the mesh you write in KPOINTS.
A finer mesh samples the zone better and costs more time, because each k-point is a separate calculation.
How fine is fine enough is found by testing, not by a fixed rule.

title: Bands and the density of states
alt: Energy levels of a toy crystal drawn as bands, or as a density of states, with a gap between the bands.
sentences: The allowed electron energies in a crystal form bands, ranges of energy with many states, separated by gaps with none.
A band structure plots those energies along a path through the zone, and the density of states counts how many states sit at each energy.
Whether the Fermi level lies in a gap or inside a band tells you if a material is an insulator or a metal; the picture is a toy model.

title: Spin up and down, and magnetic orderings
alt: Eight atoms in a cube each carrying an arrow for the direction of its magnetic moment, arranged as ferromagnetic or as A, C or G type antiferromagnetic.
sentences: Electrons carry spin, so a magnetic atom acts like a tiny arrow, and VASP follows spin up and spin down separately when you set ISPIN = 2.
Neighbouring arrows can all point the same way (ferromagnetic) or alternate in the patterns called A, C and G antiferromagnetic.
The picture is a hand-set arrangement of arrows and not a result: which pattern has the lowest energy is for a calculation to say.

title: Your first VASP folder
alt: Flow diagram of the four input files in a VASP folder, POSCAR, INCAR, KPOINTS and POTCAR, going into the program that writes the output files.
sentences: A VASP run reads four input files from one folder: POSCAR, INCAR, KPOINTS and POTCAR.
POSCAR holds the structure, INCAR the settings, KPOINTS the sampling mesh and POTCAR the pseudopotentials.
The Input Builder writes the first three for you; POTCAR comes from your VASP licence and this site never hosts it.
